source.note: Original equivalent activities; not verbatim textbook exercises.

concepts.name: Cover the inside
concepts.teach: Area tells how much flat space is inside a figure. Imagine covering the face of a classroom board with square paper. The paper covers the inside.
concepts.alternative: Imagine coloring a shape. Area measures the surface you color. The line around it is its boundary.

check.question: Does area measure the inside surface or the boundary?

example.text: Think of a small picture frame. The squares cover the picture inside. The frame around the edge is the boundary.

concepts.name: One little square
concepts.teach: Each side of a unit square is one unit long. Equal unit squares give us a consistent way to measure a surface.
concepts.alternative: A unit is a chosen length. A unit square is one unit across and one unit tall. All our measuring squares must be the same size.

check.question: How long is each side of a unit square?

example.text: This single measuring square is one unit across and one unit tall. It covers one square unit.

concepts.name: Cover without gaps
concepts.teach: Tiling means covering a figure with unit squares, without gaps or overlaps. Gaps leave surface uncovered. Overlaps cover some surface twice.
concepts.alternative: Imagine laying square stickers on a card. They must meet edge to edge. No bare spots, and no sticker on top of another.

check.question: Why would a gap make our area count inaccurate?

example.text: These squares have spaces between them. Some of the surface is uncovered, so this is not a valid tiling.

followUp.question: If we leave part of a surface uncovered, what happens to the measurement?
options: It misses some of the surface
followUp.answer: It misses some of the surface

concepts.name: Count every square
concepts.teach: Each tile represents one square unit. Count every square exactly once. You can count across one row, then the next.
concepts.alternative: Touch each square as you count. Move to a new row after reaching the end. Say square units with your total.

check.question: What is the area of this figure in square units?

example.text: Count the top row: one, two, three. Keep counting in the bottom row: four, five, six. Six squares cover six square units.

concepts.name: Finish the tiling
concepts.teach: Some squares are missing from this tiling. The outline still shows the whole figure. Add equal unit squares until the whole inside is covered.
concepts.alternative: Use a shown square as a guide. Extend its edges across the blank space. Count both the original squares and the ones you add.

check.question: Complete the tiling by tapping the blank spaces. Then what is the whole area in square units?

example.text: Finish covering the whole figure before counting. This smaller completed example has two rows of three squares: six square units.

concepts.name: Follow the outline
concepts.teach: Not every figure is a rectangle. Tile only the surface inside this outline. Empty space outside the outline is not part of the figure.
concepts.alternative: This figure has a shorter top row. Count each row separately, including only squares that belong to the figure.

check.question: What is the area inside this outline in square units?

example.text: This figure has two squares in its top row and three in its bottom row. Count only the five squares inside the figure.

concepts.name: Build an area
concepts.teach: We can also start with an area and build a figure. Each square you place contributes one square unit. Keep the squares connected edge to edge.
concepts.alternative: For an area of four square units, you could join four equal squares. Many outlines can have the same area.

check.question: Tap squares to build any connected figure with an area of 8 square units. Then send your answer.

example.text: Four squares can make a square figure or a long row. This example uses four squares in one row. Each square contributes one square unit.

concepts.name: Squares along an edge
concepts.teach: Each unit square is one unit wide. If four unit squares sit side by side along an edge, that edge is four units long. Length uses units; area uses square units.
concepts.alternative: Trace the top edge with your finger. Each square adds one unit to that edge. Count the squares across, not all the squares inside.

check.question: How many units long is the top edge of this figure?

example.text: Three unit squares side by side make an edge three units long. This entire two-row figure covers six square units.

concepts.name: Explain your thinking
concepts.teach: Equal squares fit together edge to edge to cover a surface. Circles leave spaces between them. Tiling helps us measure all of the inside once.
concepts.alternative: The job is to cover the entire surface exactly once. Square sides meet neatly. Round tiles leave uncovered spaces.

check.question: Why are unit squares better than circles for tiling a figure?

example.text: Round tiles leave spaces between them. The spaces are part of the surface too. Equal squares can meet edge to edge.

followUp.question: Which tiles can meet edge to edge without leaving spaces?

assessment.question: Find the area in square units.
assessment.feedback: Count each unit square once, row by row. State the total in square units.

assessment.question: Which rule gives a valid area measurement?
options: Use equal unit squares with no gaps or overlaps
assessment.answer: Use equal unit squares with no gaps or overlaps
assessment.feedback: Use equal unit squares. Cover the entire inside once, with no gaps or overlaps.

assessment.question: Complete this tiling. What is the whole area in square units?
assessment.feedback: Complete every blank space, then count both the original squares and the new squares.

assessment.question: Find the area inside this outline in square units.
assessment.feedback: Count only the squares inside the figure. Empty space outside does not count.

assessment.question: How many units long is each side of a unit square?
assessment.feedback: Each side of a unit square is 1 unit long. Its area is 1 square unit.

assessment.question: Build any connected figure with an area of 6 square units. Then send your answer.
assessment.feedback: Choose the requested number of squares and connect them edge to edge. More than one outline can be correct.

assessment.question: How many units long is the top edge?
assessment.feedback: Count only the unit squares along the top edge. Edge length uses units, not square units.

assessment.question: Explain how tiling helps you find area, and why gaps or overlaps change the measurement.
assessment.feedback: Look for an explanation that tiling measures the entire inside once. Gaps miss surface; overlaps count some surface twice.
